faqs.a: Classless Inter-Domain Routing. It is the compact way to describe a block of IP addresses: the address followed by a slash and the number of network bits, for example 192.168.0.0/24.
You can type an address with host bits set, for example 192.168.0.77/24. The tool normalizes it to the true network address (192.168.0.0/24) and tells you it did so.
faqs.q: Do I have to enter the exact network address?

faqs.a: It means the address block is divided into smaller equal blocks. Each extra prefix bit doubles the number of subnets and halves their size: a /24 split into /26 gives 4 subnets of 64 addresses each.
faqs.q: What does splitting a subnet mean?

faqs.a: Yes - it accepts any prefix from /0 (the entire IPv4 space) to /32 (a single host). Very large splits are capped at 256 displayed rows so the page stays fast.
faqs.q: Can it handle very large blocks like /8?

faqs.a: Cloud VPCs, Docker networks, VPN tunnels, firewall rules, and Kubernetes pod CIDRs all use this notation. Anywhere you see a slash after an IP address, this tool decodes it.

cidr-calculator.formula:
addresses in block = 2^(32 - prefix)
subnets when splitting /P into /Q = 2^(Q - P)
size of each new subnet = 2^(32 - Q)
Example: splitting /24 into /26 -> 2^(26-24) = 4 subnets, each 2^(32-26) = 64 addresses.
howTo: Type a CIDR block such as 192.168.0.0/24 - an IPv4 address, a slash, and a prefix from 0 to 32.
Read the decoded block: network, broadcast, mask, wildcard, and first/last usable host.
If the address had host bits set, the tool normalizes it to the true network address automatically.
To split the block, choose a longer new prefix - each extra bit doubles the subnet count.
Scan the generated subnet list for exact boundaries before pasting them into your configs.
keyFacts: CIDR notation = an IP address, a slash, and a prefix length: 192.168.0.0/24 means the first 24 bits are the network.
A /P block always contains exactly 2^(32-P) addresses: /24 = 256, /16 = 65,536, /8 = 16,777,216.
Splitting a /P block into /Q subnets yields 2^(Q-P) subnets, each with 2^(32-Q) addresses.
The host portion of the entered address is ignored for the math - only the network bits define the block.
Common blocks: /32 single host, /31 point-to-point link, /30 four addresses, /24 a classic LAN, /16 a large site.
CIDR replaced classful A/B/C addressing in 1993; classes are historical reference only.

limitations: IPv4 only. IPv6 CIDR (for example 2001:db8::/32) uses 128-bit math this tool does not implement.
Splitting is limited to 256 displayed subnets; enormous splits show the first 256.
It computes address boundaries, not routing: overlapping with existing routes is still your responsibility to check.
Normalization silently drops host bits - double-check the block matches what you intended before deploying.
